323.title: Mary, mother of the Church (CCC 963–970)
323.hook: her role points always to her son
323.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary on its own and in the rosary, and since 2018 keep the memorial of Mary, Mother of the Church, on the Monday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, communio sanctorum: the living, the dead and the saints, one family. Your line was one family. Today, the one Catholics call the mother of that family.

There's a kind of icon, very old, that you'll find in Greek, Russian and Catholic churches alike. Mary holds the child Jesus on one arm. Her face isn't turned to you, exactly. Her other hand is open, palm up, gesturing toward the child. The icon's Greek name is Hodegetria: she who shows the way. People sometimes imagine Catholic devotion to Mary as a spotlight on her. In this picture, she's pointing away from herself.
screen: `AN OLD ICON.` → `HER HAND POINTS TO THE CHILD.` → `SHE WHO SHOWS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Start at a wedding in Cana. The wine runs out. Mary tells Jesus, then turns to the servants and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." It's the last thing John's Gospel records her saying. Not look at me. Do what he tells you. Then the cross. Jesus sees his mother and the disciple he loved standing by. "Woman, behold thy son." Then to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." From that hour, John says, the disciple took her into his own home. Catholics read that disciple as standing for every believer: Jesus giving his mother to the whole Church. During the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul VI gave her the title Mother of the Church. The Catechism says her place in the Church can't be separated from her union with Christ. It calls her the Church's model of faith and love, who prays for the Church as a mother prays for her children. And it's careful: her role in no way hides or takes away from Christ as the one mediator. It shows his power. Here Christians differ. Orthodox Christians honor her deeply as Theotokos, God-bearer, and ask her prayers too. Many Protestants honor her as the mother of Jesus and a model of faith, but don't pray to her. Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with the angel's greeting in Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." And at its middle, the prayer names her son: Jesus.

segments.voice: If you pray it, pray one Hail Mary slowly for the whole Church, its people, its wounds, its saints and sinners, giving each phrase a breath. If you don't, picture the old icon instead: the mother, the child, the open hand. Follow where the hand points, and rest your attention there.
Mary. The mother of Jesus, whom Catholics call Mother of the Church: a model of faith, whose whole role, the Church says, is to point to her son. Today's word.

324.title: Death (CCC 1005–1014)
324.howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with the words remember that you are dust, pray for a holy death, and many keep November as a month of remembering the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary: the mother whose hand points to her son. Your line was she points to him. Today, the last things begin: death, judgment, and what comes after.

Ash Wednesday. A line shuffles toward the front of the church: office workers on a lunch break, kids in school uniforms, an old man with a cane. One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb of gray ash onto each forehead, in the shape of a cross, and says a sentence nobody would put on a greeting card: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. Nobody is required to come. The line still reaches the back door. Why would Catholics want that reminder?
screen: `ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `YOU ARE DUST.` → `PEOPLE LINE UP FOR IT.`

segments.voice: The words are God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In Latin, memento, homo, quia pulvis es: remember, human, that you are dust. That word memento, remember, gives today's phrase: memento mori, remember that you will die. The Catechism is honest about death. It's the end of earthly life, and it's natural, and in Christian teaching it's also a consequence of sin, something God did not originally want for human beings. But Christ, it says, has changed its meaning. Because he died and rose, Catholics say, death is no longer only an end. It can be a passage. Paul could write to the Philippians of "having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ." And tradition says that Francis of Assisi, near his own death, added a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising God for our Sister Death. So why remember it? Not to be morbid. The Catechism says remembering death reminds people that their time to make something of their lives is limited. The old litany of the saints even asks to be spared a sudden and unprepared death: not to be spared death, but to meet it ready. Remembering changes a Tuesday: the grudge looks smaller, the phone call to your mother looks bigger. Old paintings of saints at prayer sometimes put a skull on the desk, beside the book and the candle. Not fear. Focus.

segments.voice: Imagine, gently, the day people gather to remember you: not the sad part, just the words. What would you want someone who loved you to say, not your job title, but something like she always had time, he made people laugh, they never gave up on anyone? Let one sentence come and hold it; if you pray, you can ask for help to become it.
Memento mori. Latin for remember that you will die: an old Christian practice of keeping death in view, not out of fear, but to live well. Today's word.
Your line: remember you will die. Ash Wednesday says it once a year; your line can say it any day. See you tomorrow.

325.title: Judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
325.hook: at death each person is judged by love
325.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and many make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day with the question of how they loved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, memento mori: remembering death to live well. Your line was remember you will die. Today, what Catholics say happens the moment after.

A courtroom. A huge book. Every lie you ever told, read out loud. A stern face, a gavel. Maybe a scale, good deeds on one side and bad ones on the other, and you watching to see which way it tips. That's what the word judgment can drag in. Now hold it next to a sentence from a Spanish friar you met earlier on this path, John of the Cross: at the evening of life, he said, we will be judged on love. Not on the scale. On love.
screen: `A COURTROOM, A BOOK, A GAVEL.` → `A SCALE THAT TIPS.` → `JUDGED ON LOVE.`

segments.voice: Hebrews says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." The Catechism teaches that each person receives this judgment at the very moment of death. It's called the particular judgment, because it's about one particular life. And it's immediate. At death, the Catechism says, each soul receives its eternal destiny at once: heaven, either through a purification or directly, or else separation from God forever. Catholics point to the thief crucified next to Jesus, who asked only to be remembered, and heard: "this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Not someday. Today. The Catechism quotes John of the Cross's line about being judged on love at the evening of life. It fits Jesus's own story of the sheep and the goats, where the question isn't how much you knew but whether you fed the hungry. Catholics say that at death a person sees their life in Christ's light, and the question is how they loved, and whether they accepted or refused his love. The Church also speaks of a final judgment at the end of time, when Christ returns and the whole of history is brought into the light. The particular judgment is one life. The last judgment is all of them together. And the one who judges, Catholics say, is the same one who died for the person being judged: justice, yes, but from a judge who wants each person home.

segments.voice: Choose one person close to you, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, a coworker, and look at the last month with them, honestly but kindly. Where did you love well, and where did love run thin, a short word, a missed call, a silence? Name both without beating yourself up, then ask what more love would look like here this week; if you pray, you can ask for help to do it.
Judgment. In Catholic teaching, the moment at death when each life is seen in Christ's light, and judged on love, followed by a final judgment at the end of time. Today's word.
Your line: judged by love. On love, not on a scale. Day three hundred twenty-five, done.

326.title: Purgatory (CCC 1030–1032)
326.hook: a purifying for those who die in God's friendship but not yet whole
326.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass, have Masses offered for loved ones who have died, and keep All Souls Day on November 2, when many visit cemeteries to pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: judged by love. Today, those who die loving God but not yet whole.

The invitation says seven. The host is someone you love. It's ten to seven; you've been gardening all day: dirt under your nails, sweat, a scratch on your arm. You're welcome as you are; the invitation is real and isn't taken back. But at the door you might still say: give me a minute, let me wash first. That wanting to be clean first is close to what the Church means by a word often heard as something darker.
screen: `INVITED TO THE DINNER.` → `COVERED IN DIRT.` → `LET ME WASH FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation. After death they undergo a purification, to gain the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Church calls it purgatory, from the Latin purgare: to cleanse. It isn't a second chance for someone who refused God, or a smaller hell; the Catechism says it's entirely different from the punishment of the damned. Everyone there is already saved, on the way in. Catholics point to Paul: a person whose work burns up "shall be saved, yet so as by fire." And to Second Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." The Church, the Catechism says, has prayed for the dead from the beginning. Orthodox Christians pray for their dead too, without defining a purgatory in the same way; many Protestants don't hold the teaching. One mix-up: purgatory isn't limbo. Limbo was a theory some theologians held about babies who die before baptism; the Church never made it a teaching. The Catechism entrusts those children to God's mercy, with hope for their salvation. If that loss is yours, you don't have to carry it alone; in the US, 988 answers day and night. Tradition speaks of a cleansing fire, and Benedict XVI suggested the fire might be Christ himself: meeting his gaze burns away what's false, and that pain is the pain of love, which heals. On this view, purgatory isn't about being punished enough. It's about being loved until a person is whole.
screen: `PURGARE: TO CLEANSE.` · `ALREADY SAVED, ON THE WAY IN.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `THE FIRE MAY BE HIS GAZE.` · then, large: `PURIFIED BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think of the dead nobody names: a worn stone in an old cemetery where the name has rubbed away, the person who lived in your home before you. No one may be thinking of them today. If you pray, hold them in the old prayer for the dead or a few words of your own; if not, hold them in mind and wish them whole.
Purgatory. From the Latin for cleansing: the final purification, Catholics believe, of those who die in God's friendship but aren't yet whole. Today's word.
Your line: purified by love. Not a smaller hell, but a washing before the dinner. Until tomorrow.

327.title: Hell (CCC 1033–1037)
327.hook: the Church teaches it as self-exclusion from God, and prays that none be lost
327.howItsDone: At Mass the Church prays to be saved from final damnation, and many Catholics add the Fatima prayer to each decade of the rosary, asking that all souls be led to heaven, especially those most in need of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purgatory: a cleansing for those already on their way into heaven. Your line was purified by love. Today, the hardest of the last things, told carefully.

Outside the old walls of Jerusalem there's a valley. Its Hebrew name is Ge Hinnom, the valley of Hinnom. In the Bible's darkest chapters it was a place of terrible worship, and the prophets cursed it. Later, tradition says, it became associated with burning and refuse. When Jesus warned his listeners about the ultimate loss, he used that valley's name. In Greek it became Gehenna, and English Bibles usually translate it as hell. So the word starts with a real place people could point to.
screen: `A VALLEY OUTSIDE JERUSALEM.` → `GE HINNOM, GEHENNA.` → `A REAL PLACE, A WARNING.`

segments.voice: Jesus speaks about hell often in the Gospels, and the Church takes his warnings seriously. The Catechism defines hell as a state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God and the blessed. Not a trap God springs on people: a final, free refusal of love. Why is it possible at all? The Catechism says no one can be united with God unless they freely choose to love him. Love can't be forced. If a person can truly say yes, they can truly say no. The chief pain of hell, the Church says, is being separated from God, the only one in whom a human being can find the life and happiness they were made for. And no one is sent there by design. The Catechism states that God predestines no one to go to hell; it takes a willful turning away, persisted in to the end. The Gospel's warnings, it says, are a call to responsibility and to conversion, not a threat meant to frighten. So the Church prays that no one be lost, leaning on two verses. First Timothy: God "will have all men to be saved." And Second Peter: the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance." At every Mass using the Roman Canon, the Church asks to be saved from final damnation. It has declared many people saints, in heaven. It has never declared any particular person to be in hell. Catholics hold two things together: the teaching is real, and the Church prays for all.
screen: `SELF-EXCLUSION, NOT A TRAP.` · `LOVE CAN'T BE FORCED.` · `GOD PREDESTINES NO ONE TO HELL.` · `THE CHURCH PRAYS NONE BE LOST.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH PRAYS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who seems lost, or hard, or turned away: someone you know, or someone in the news whose cruelty you can't understand. Don't excuse what they've done; just hold them in mind as a person God made. If you pray, ask God to have mercy on them and bring them home; if you don't, simply wish them turned toward the good.
Hell. In Catholic teaching, the state of definitive self-exclusion from God, a final refusal of love, and the reason the Church prays that no one be lost. Today's word.
Your line: the church prays for all. Even the ones hardest to pray for. That's three hundred twenty-seven days.

328.title: Heaven (CCC 1023–1029)
328.hook: seeing God face to face, beyond what eye has seen
328.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead that they may see God's face, keep All Saints Day on November 1 for all who are in heaven, and at funerals the Church sings In Paradisum, asking that the angels lead the dead into paradise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hell: a final refusal of love, and the Church's prayer that no one be lost. Your line was the church prays for all. Today, what that prayer is hoping for.

Clouds. Harps. Everyone in white robes, a bit bored, forever. That's the cartoon heaven, and no wonder some call it dull. Set a different scene next to it. An airport arrivals gate, late at night. The doors slide open, and someone you love, someone you haven't seen in years, comes around the corner. Your eyes meet. For one second the noise of the hall drops away. Catholic teaching about heaven has almost nothing to do with the clouds and everything to do with that second: a face, seen at last, and never lost again.
screen: `CLOUDS, HARPS, WHITE ROBES.` → `AN ARRIVALS GATE.` → `A FACE, SEEN AT LAST.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Now the seeing is dim, like a reflection in a glass. Then, direct. First John adds: "we shall see him as he is." The Church calls this seeing the beatific vision, from the Latin visio beatifica: the vision that makes you happy. The Catechism describes heaven as perfect life with the Trinity, a communion of life and love with God, Mary, the angels and all the blessed. It calls heaven the fulfillment of the deepest longings of the human heart. Augustine said it at the start of his Confessions: "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Heaven, for Catholics, is that rest. The Catechism admits this mystery goes beyond any understanding or description. So Scripture uses pictures: life, light, peace, a wedding feast, the Father's house, a city. Paul reaches for an older scripture: "That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him." Each image points somewhere; none is enough on its own. And it isn't boring. Seeing God, Catholics say, isn't staring at a wall forever. Some Catholic writers describe it as endless discovery of one who has no end, shared with all the blessed. Face to face with God, and so, many Catholics hope, face to face again with those they've lost.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, to death or to distance, and picture them coming toward you, at the arrivals gate, a kitchen door, a field: their face, the way they'd say your name. Let yourself feel it, even if it aches; Catholics hope for this and more, that every good meeting is a hint of seeing God. If you pray, thank God for that person.
Beatific vision. From the Latin for the vision that makes happy: seeing God face to face, which Catholics believe is the heart of heaven. Today's word.

329.title: The resurrection of the body (CCC 988–1004)
329.hook: Catholics believe the whole person, body too, will be raised
329.howItsDone: Catholics profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, bury their dead or reverently inter their ashes in consecrated places rather than scattering them, and honor the body in funeral rites as one day to be raised.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. Your line was face to face. Today, the line in the Creed that says the face itself, and the body it belongs to, has a future too.

A bird flies out of an open cage, and the cage is left on the floor. A coat is shrugged off at the door and left on the hook. People sometimes reach for those pictures when they talk about death: the soul goes free, the body stays behind. But in the Apostles' Creed, just before the last line, Christians say something stranger and more physical. Not only the survival of the soul. Something about bodies: hands, faces, the scar on your knee. The Catholic Church says the coat isn't thrown away.
screen: `A BIRD OUT OF A CAGE?` → `AN OLD COAT LEFT BEHIND?` → `HANDS, FACES, SCARS.`

segments.voice: In English the Creed ends: the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. The Latin is even blunter: carnis resurrectionem, the resurrection of the flesh. Why the body? The Catechism says a human being is one: body and soul together, not a soul trapped in a body. So salvation, in Catholic teaching, isn't escape from the body. It's the whole person, raised. The early writer Tertullian made a Latin pun: caro salutis est cardo. The flesh is the hinge of salvation. Remember cardo, the hinge, from the four virtues? Catholics say God took flesh, was raised in the flesh, and will raise ours. What kind of body? Not a corpse stitched back together. Paul compares it to a seed and the plant it becomes: the same life, utterly changed. In the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The Catechism says the dead will rise with their own bodies, the ones they have now, but changed, like Christ's glorious body, no longer able to die. How exactly, it says, goes beyond human imagination and understanding. When: on the last day, when Christ returns. And if the body has a future, it isn't disposable. Paul says "your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost." So Catholics are asked to respect their own bodies and everyone else's: the sick body, the aging body, the body in the grave.

segments.voice: Start at your feet, which have carried you everywhere, and thank them; then your hands that have held people, your lungs filling right now without being asked, your heart beating since before you were born. Notice any part that hurts, or that you've been unkind to in your head, and thank that part too. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you've been given.
Carnis resurrectionem, the Creed's Latin for the resurrection of the flesh: the whole person, body too, raised and transformed like Christ. Today's word.
Your line: the body too. The week ran from Mary through the last things, death, judgment, purgatory, hell, heaven, and now the body too. Day three hundred twenty-nine: a week, done.
